steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Thread IDs" section of an encyclopedia article on the Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) bus: what thread IDs are for, how an AXI switch handles them, and how AXI-Lite differs from full AXI.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What thread IDs do: multiple threads per initiator port, ordering rules
- Examples of thread ordering
- Thread IDs in an AXI switch
- AXI-Lite vs. full AXI
- Note: AXI-Lite transaction length

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- What thread IDs do
  - single initiator port, multiple threads
  - in-order access to AXI address space within a thread
  - different thread IDs from same port may complete out of order w.r.t. each other
- Examples
  - one thread ID blocked by slow peripheral -> another continues independently
  - CPU thread with its own initiator port thread ID: read addr1, write addr1, read addr1 -> completes in order (same ID)
  - other CPU thread, other ID: also in order, but may be intermixed with first thread's transactions
- AXI switch
  - thread IDs not globally defined on an initiator port
  - switch with multiple initiator ports prefixes initiator port index to thread ID
  - concatenated ID given to target device
  - on return: prefix used to locate initiator port of origin, then truncated
  - hence target port thread ID wider in bits than initiator port thread ID
- AXI-Lite vs. full AXI
  - AXI-Lite: single ID thread per initiator
  - for end points talking to one initiator at a time, e.g. simple peripheral like UART
  - CPU: transactions to multiple peripherals/address spaces at a time, >1 thread ID on initiator and target ports -> full spec AXI
  - typical front side AXI switch: full spec AXI initiator connected to CPU initiator, several AXI-Lite targets from peripherals
- AXI-Lite also limited to single data word per transaction

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Thread IDs let one initiator port support more than one thread. Each thread gets in-order access to the AXI address space, but the different thread IDs coming from the same initiator port can complete out of order compared to each other. For example, if one thread ID is blocked by a slow peripheral, another thread ID can keep going, independent of the order of the first one. As another example, a thread on a CPU could be given a thread ID for a certain initiator port memory access, like read addr1, write addr1, read addr1, and this sequence completes in order because every transaction has the same initiator port thread ID. A different thread on the CPU can have a different initiator port thread ID, and its memory accesses are also in order, but they can be mixed in with the transactions of the first thread ID.

Thread IDs on an initiator port are not defined globally. So an AXI switch that has several initiator ports will add the initiator port index as a prefix to the thread ID internally and pass this combined thread ID on to the target device. When the transaction comes back, the switch uses this prefix to find which initiator port it came from, and then the prefix is cut off. That is the reason the thread ID on the target port has more bits than the thread ID on the initiator port.

- AXI-Lite: AXI bus with only a single ID thread per initiator
  - used for end point that only talks to one initiator at a time, e.g. simple peripheral like a UART
  - CPU: transactions to multiple peripherals and address spaces at a time, more than one thread ID on AXI initiator and target ports -> full spec AXI bus
  - typical front side AXI switch: full spec AXI initiator connected to CPU initiator + several AXI-Lite targets from different peripherals
- AXI-Lite: only single data word per transaction

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Thread IDs let one initiator port support more than one thread. Each thread gets in-order access to the AXI address space, but the different thread IDs coming from the same initiator port can complete out of order compared to each other. For example, if one thread ID is blocked by a slow peripheral, another thread ID can keep going, independent of the order of the first one. As another example, a thread on a CPU could be given a thread ID for a certain initiator port memory access, like read addr1, write addr1, read addr1, and this sequence completes in order because every transaction has the same initiator port thread ID. A different thread on the CPU can have a different initiator port thread ID, and its memory accesses are also in order, but they can be mixed in with the transactions of the first thread ID.

Thread IDs on an initiator port are not defined globally. So an AXI switch that has several initiator ports will add the initiator port index as a prefix to the thread ID internally and pass this combined thread ID on to the target device. When the transaction comes back, the switch uses this prefix to find which initiator port it came from, and then the prefix is cut off. That is the reason the thread ID on the target port has more bits than the thread ID on the initiator port.

AXI-Lite is an AXI bus that only supports one ID thread per initiator. It is usually used for an end point that only has to talk to one initiator device at a time, for example a simple peripheral like a UART. A CPU on the other hand can start transactions to several peripherals and address spaces at once, and it will support more than one thread ID on its AXI initiator ports and AXI target ports. This is why a CPU usually supports a full spec AXI bus. A typical front side AXI switch would have a full specification AXI initiator connected to a CPU initiator, and several AXI-Lite targets from different peripheral devices connected to the switch.

Also, the AXI-Lite bus only supports transactions of a single data word each.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Thread IDs allow a single initiator port to support multiple threads, where each thread has in-order access to the AXI address space, but each thread ID initiated from a single initiator port may complete out of order with respect to the others. For instance, if one thread ID is blocked by a slow peripheral, another thread ID may continue independently of the order of the first thread ID. As another example, one thread on a CPU may be assigned a thread ID for a particular initiator port memory access such as read addr1, write addr1, read addr1, and this sequence will complete in order because each transaction has the same initiator port thread ID. Another thread running on the CPU may have a different initiator port thread ID assigned to it, and its memory accesses will be in order as well, but may be intermixed with the transactions of the first thread ID.[1]

Thread IDs on an initiator port are not globally defined, so an AXI switch with multiple initiator ports will internally prefix the initiator port index to the thread ID and provide this concatenated thread ID to the target device. When the transaction returns to its initiator port of origin, the prefix is used to locate the initiator port and is then truncated. This is why the target port thread ID is wider in bits than the initiator port thread ID.[2]

The AXI-Lite bus is an AXI bus that only supports a single ID thread per initiator. It is typically used for an end point that only needs to communicate with a single initiator device at a time, for example a simple peripheral such as a UART. A CPU, by contrast, can initiate transactions to multiple peripherals and address spaces at a time, and will support more than one thread ID on its AXI initiator ports and AXI target ports, which is why a CPU will typically support a full spec AXI bus. A typical front side AXI switch would include a full specification AXI initiator connected to a CPU initiator, and several AXI-Lite targets from different peripheral devices connected to the AXI switch.[3]

(The AXI-Lite bus is also restricted to transaction lengths of a single data word per transaction.)

References:
[1] (22 February 2013). AMBA AXI and ACE Protocol Specification. Arm Ltd.. https://developer.arm.com/-/media/Arm%20Developer%20Community/PDF/IHI0022H_amba_axi_protocol_spec.pdf
[2] (17 May 2022). AXI Interconnect v2.1 LogiCORE IP Product Guide. Xilinx. https://www.xilinx.com/support/documents/ip_documentation/axi_interconnect/v2_1/pg059-axi-interconnect.pdf
[3] (2021). AXI Thread IDs (TIDs) – SoC Basics. Institute for Embedded Systems, TU Graz. https://www.isec.tugraz.at/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/p2.pdf
